inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Imagine asking an AI which doors are missing a fire rating. It gives you a perfect table. There's just one problem: none of those doors exist in your model.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Then how do you get an answer you can actually check?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: [warmly] Welcome back to Insights. I'm Martin Motlík. I work where software meets structural engineering. Today we're looking at the Model Context Protocol, or M-C-P, through a model-review test I built myself.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Sarah is back as our fictional marketing lead at an engineering firm in Portland. Her boss has a question.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: He's forwarded another vendor email: "Should we be doing this M-C-P thing?" I need an answer I can take back to the team.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Let's work through it. What can it do, what still needs checking, and where would you start?

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Okay, start from zero. What is it?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: M-C-P is an open standard that lets AI apps connect to the software and data you already use. It doesn't make the AI smarter. It gives it a way to reach things outside itself. Your models, your analysis software, your project data.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: So, a plug.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Pretty much. Picture the temporary power spider box on a jobsite. It doesn't care if you plug in a saw, a grinder or a work light, because every tool has the same plug. Before M-C-P, connecting an AI to a program meant custom wiring for every single pair.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And now?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Now software can expose its tools through an M-C-P server, and compatible AI apps can connect to it. You still need the right connection and permissions. Anthropic introduced the standard in late 2024.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: We pay for Copilot. So in that picture, Copilot is...

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: The host. The app you type into. On the other side, a small server sits next to Revit, or next to the tool that reads your I-F-C files, and tells the AI what it can do.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Tells it how?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Each tool has a description and a structured definition of its inputs. The AI uses those to choose a tool and supply the information it needs. The application controls which tools are available.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: So back to the doors. What would have been different?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: The AI would have a way to query the actual model. A tool can open the I-F-C file, find the doors and return their properties. We can check those results. The AI can still choose the wrong filter or misread an answer, so the connection alone doesn't make it reliable.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: So the AI is more of a coordinator.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Exactly. Like a good BIM coordinator, actually. It doesn't author the model. It knows where to look, and it brings back the answer.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: But here's the thing. Copilot already reads our documents. Our BIM Execution Plan, our standards. Isn't that the same?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: That's a different tool, and a good one. The AI searches documents and quotes them. It answers "what does the BIM Execution Plan say?"

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And M-C-P?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: M-C-P can connect both kinds of tools. One searches your documents; another queries the model or runs a check. The useful difference is what the tool can do. Most serious workflows will use both.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Give me something real. What would our team actually ask?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Find the doors on level two with a missing fire-rating property, and show me where they are. Or total the concrete quantities in the slabs, floor by floor, if the model contains reliable quantities. Those are questions the connected tools can answer.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: [laughs] And the doors would have been real doors.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Can I be honest? Everything I read about this is a vendor demo. Have you actually tried it yourself?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: I have. I'm building a model-review prototype, a web app for I-F-C models. It already checks models against information requirements and compares versions. So I wrote a small M-C-P server for it. Six tools, all read-only.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Read-only meaning...

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: It can look, it can't touch. List elements, read their properties, run a check, compare two revisions, and hand me a link into the 3D viewer. That's it.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: But couldn't your model checker already do that without AI?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Yes. The checker already did the validation. What I added was a way to ask follow-up questions, connect the steps, and jump straight to the affected elements.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And what did you test it on?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: A real model. A residential building in Prague, a concept model with a garage, three apartment floors and an attic. Plus an I-D-S file with the project's data requirements.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: I-D-S. Remind me?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: I-D-S is a buildingSMART standard for expressing selected information requirements in a machine-checkable form. You specify which elements need which data. A checker then tests the model against those rules. It checks the information, not whether the building is correctly designed.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Oh. That's literally what our BIM coordinator does every Friday before a submittal. By hand.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Then she'll like this part. I asked: check the model against the I-D-S file. Which requirements fail, and which elements are affected? Two requirements failed. Thirteen elements, mostly doors without a fire rating.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Doors with no fire rating. That sounds bad.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: The door names said the fire rating would be set in the fire safety design. That explained why the value was missing. It didn't actually provide a fire rating.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: So the check found a real gap, but it didn't tell you whether the design was wrong.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Exactly. You also need to know whether that information is required at this project stage. The check flags the missing value. A person decides what it means.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Then what?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Then I prepared a second revision for the test, with some of the gaps filled in. And I asked the question every team asks after a revision: what got fixed, and what's still missing? Show me the rest in the model.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: The AI called the comparison and validation tools, and the results were matched by element ID. Ten of thirteen fixed. Three doors on residential level three still without a fire rating. Then it gave me a link that opened the model, and there they were. Three doors highlighted, the rest of the building dimmed.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: [surprised] So the doors in the chat and the doors on screen are the same doors.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Same element IDs. That's the part I'd show any project team first.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Okay, but which AI did you use? We're a Copilot shop.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: I tested the same server with ChatGPT and with Gemini in Google Antigravity. In that test, both reached the same findings. That doesn't mean every AI app connects in the same way. With Copilot, you need to check the specific product and your company's setup.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Was building the server the hard part?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Writing the code wasn't the hard part.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: What was?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Three things. First, the tool descriptions. The AI picks tools by reading them, so they're really the user interface. They deserve the same care as button labels.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: [laughs] Copywriting. Finally something in my lane.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Honestly, yes. Second, summaries beat data dumps. Return counts and the top results, with details on request. Send an AI a whole model and you overload its working memory. The answers get worse.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And third?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Units and IDs, always. Every number carries its unit, every element its ID. Ambiguity is exactly where the AI starts guessing again.

scene: 7 · "Why give our data to big tech?"

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Here's where I push back a bit. Why would we connect our projects to OpenAI or Google or Microsoft? Wouldn't it be safer to build our own chatbot?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Fair question. Let me separate two things: where the model lives, and where the answers go. A local server keeps the model file on your machine. Only what the tools return goes to the AI.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Which can still be a lot.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: It can. So check your provider's terms on data retention and training before you connect live projects. And some clients and contracts don't allow commercial AI services at all. Then you don't.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Okay. And the chatbot idea?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Building your own chatbot doesn't mean building your own language model. You can use the same commercial models behind a custom interface. The question is whether that interface solves a real problem for your team. M-C-P lets you reuse the engineering tools either way.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And my engineers already have Copilot open all day.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Then it makes sense to start with the interface they already use, if it supports the connection you need. A custom assistant may still be useful for a specific workflow.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: So it's not either-or.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: No. Keep the engineering tools reusable, then choose the interface that works for your team.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Okay, confession number two. One of our younger engineers found a community Revit server on GitHub and hooked it up to ChatGPT over the weekend. On a live project.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Of course he did.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Our IT guy is not amused.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Your IT guy has a point. I separate three kinds of access. First, reading: querying the model and pulling properties. That limits changes to the model, but the information can still be sensitive.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And the second?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Checking: I-D-S checks, clash reports, comparisons between revisions. People need to review the findings because they inform decisions. Third is writing: changing parameters or moving and creating elements. That needs controlled permissions and a way to review and undo changes.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And the GitHub server?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: You need to inspect what that particular server can do and what access it has. Autodesk now offers separate read, write and experimental server options as technical previews. The capabilities and permissions matter more than the label.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Anything else I should tell IT?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Model data can contain text that tries to steer the AI. Read-only limits changes to the model; it doesn't prevent misleading answers or data exposure. Start with a trusted server, restricted access and a test model your firm has approved.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Who is actually shipping this in our industry?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Autodesk has Revit servers in technical preview. Bluebeam connects Revu with Claude. Trimble has a SketchUp connector, and Dlubal provides access to its analysis applications. The capabilities, supported clients and licenses differ. But these are actual products you can evaluate.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Do they all give the AI the same kind of access?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: No. Some expose a few defined actions. Others let the AI write scripts against an API. The reach depends on what the server exposes and the permissions behind it.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Which would you start with?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: A small set of read-only tools for one task. Scripting can go further, but you need to review and test the code. I've linked the product details in the article, because those are changing quickly.

scene: 10 · What do I tell my boss?

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: Okay. That email from my boss. And our senior engineer asked me to ask you one thing: who's liable if the AI gets it wrong?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Using AI doesn't remove the engineer's responsibility to review the result. The AI doesn't stamp drawings. How liability is allocated is a separate question for the firm's contracts and legal advice.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: So we still need a review process. What else do I write back?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: That it won't clean up your data. It automates a messy process just as faithfully as a clean one. If your parameters are inconsistent, you'll just find out faster. And that it isn't free. AI subscriptions, and sometimes API access or add-on licenses on the software side.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And then?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Then a few questions for every vendor. Do you ship an M-C-P server, official or community? Is it read-only, and are read and write separated? Where does project data go? The full list is in the article.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And how do we know if it's worth it?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Choose one recurring task and a test model your firm has approved. Compare your current workflow, including any checker you already use, with the AI-assisted version. Count the review time, missed issues and false alarms as well as the time saved. Repeat it on another revision before deciding.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: That's our Friday model check.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: That's your Friday model check.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: If you had to sum it up in one sentence?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: M-C-P lets AI reach the engineering tools we already use. We still need to verify the result.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And personally? Would you share your own models with these AI companies?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: I would. Sharing building data with AI models is how they get better at our work, and I trust the large U.S. providers with it. Your contracts still set the rules for each project. In a few years, asking an AI about a model will be as ordinary as searching Google.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: And the first question to take back to the office?

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: Pick one question you ask about a model every week. Check whether your existing software can expose the answer, and how your team would verify it.

inputs.speaker: SARAH
inputs.text: In the article, you can see the tool result and the same three doors highlighted in the model. It's on martinmotlik dot com, under Insights.

inputs.speaker: MARTIN
inputs.text: [warmly] Thanks for listening. See you in the next one.
